description: The distinctive dōtaku bronze bells of Yayoi-period Japan were large, thin-walled ritual objects found especially in western and central Honshu, often buried together in caches away from settlements. Although derived from earlier functional bells, many dōtaku became too large and delicate for everyday use and were probably employed in agricultural, seasonal, or communal ceremonies connected with fertility, harvests, and protection. Their surfaces were frequently decorated with geometric patterns, animals, hunting scenes, and images of daily life, making them important evidence for Yayoi religious symbolism and social organization during the centuries leading toward the Yamatai period.
